name: ABS-GF (Glass-Fiber-Filled ABS)
chemical_makeup: The same amorphous acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene terpolymer as base ABS, compounded with chopped glass fiber — around 10 wt% in most consumer grades (Siraya Fibreheart ABS-GF), though some third-party lines are branded 'ABS-GF25' implying up to 25 %. Glass fiber is electrically non-conductive and light-coloured, so unlike a carbon-filled grade it does not restrict the product to black.
summary: ABS with its worst habit partly cured. Deltas vs abs: glass fiber suppresses the shrinkage-driven warp that dominates unfilled ABS printing, lifting dimensional stability from 4 to 7, at the cost of a mandatory hardened nozzle and a slightly weaker interlayer bond. Heat resistance barely moves (HDT 99-106 °C against base ABS's 99 °C) and UV resistance does not move at all — this stays a poor outdoor material, which is the whole reason asa-cf exists alongside it.

printing.notes: Deltas vs base ABS: hardened nozzle now mandatory, and the nozzle window shifts slightly up (Bambu 240-270 °C, Siraya Fibreheart 250-270 °C, against base ABS's 230-270 °C). Bed guidance splits by vendor — Bambu 80-100 °C with glue, Siraya 100-110 °C — with the higher figures needed because a stiffer filled matrix cracks rather than flexes if a corner does lift. Part cooling stays essentially off, as for base ABS. Bambu states outright that an enclosed printer is required; a passive enclosure is normally sufficient, so heated_chamber_required stays false, matching the base entry. Nozzles of 0.4/0.6/0.8 mm are supported and 0.2 mm is not.

feeding.notes: The most permissive AMS answer of the five filled grades here, and the one real feeding surprise: Bambu lists its own ABS-GF as compatible with both AMS and AMS lite, where nearly every other fiber-filled filament is barred — the glass loading apparently keeps the strand ductile enough not to snap in the feed path. Third-party ABS-GF should still be assumed incompatible unless the vendor says otherwise, so this is recorded 'conditional' rather than 'yes'. Rigid, so any drive system feeds it; hardened steel nozzle required regardless of AMS use. Not flexible: no shore hardness, no feeding assistant.

drying.dryness_validation: No popping, crackling or steam at the nozzle and no micro-bubbles in the extrudate. Base ABS's 'no fine hairs or fuzz on printed walls' check is unreliable here — a fiber-filled wall is slightly fuzzy by nature — so rely on sound and on strand quality instead.
drying.notes: Bambu specifies 80 °C for 8 h; Siraya's Fibreheart grade asks for only 65 °C for 4-6 h. Both sit inside base ABS's 70-85 °C / 4-8 h band, so the glass fiber adds essentially no drying burden of its own; as with base ABS, the real practice is desiccant storage between prints rather than a pre-print ritual.

storage.recommendations: Airtight box or drybox with desiccant at all times, as for base ABS. Glass fiber does not raise the absorption rate, but the stiffer filled matrix shows moisture-driven layer defects as cracks rather than as cosmetic roughness.

price.notes: Bambu $29.99/kg. A modest premium over base ABS's $18-35/kg and by far the cheapest filled grade in this cluster — roughly a third of asa-cf's price — because glass fiber is cheaper to compound than carbon fiber and ABS resin is itself inexpensive.

recommended: mechanical parts needing dimensional accuracy from an ABS-family material
large flat ABS parts that would warp unfilled
enclosures and housings for indoor equipment
functional end-use parts on enclosed printers
parts near electronics, where the non-conductive filler matters
not_recommended: UV-exposed or outdoor parts (inherits ABS's poor UV life — use asa-cf)
printing in an unventilated occupied room (styrene fumes)
impact-critical parts (the fiber trades away some of ABS's toughness)

properties.notes: Density 1.08 g/cm³ — Bambu and Siraya Fibreheart agree — barely above base ABS's 1.05, since glass fiber is dense but the loading is low. Bambu: tensile 36±3 MPa, bending modulus 2860±130 MPa, HDT 99 °C, Vicat softening 103 °C. Siraya Fibreheart: tensile 44±3 MPa, softening 106 °C. Read the numbers as a stiffness-and-stability upgrade rather than a strength one: tensile sits inside base ABS's own 30-45 MPa band, HDT is identical to base ABS's 99 °C, and only the bending modulus (2860 MPa against roughly 2000-2300 MPa for unfilled ABS) and the warp behaviour move meaningfully. Shrinkage is a reasoned reduction from base ABS's 0.5-1.5 % on the strength of Bambu's 'minimal warping' claim, not a datasheet figure; Tg and max service temp are carried from the base entry.

compatibility.notes: Welds to itself and across the styrenic family — base ABS, base ASA and asa-cf — sharing one enclosed, hot-bed process environment. HIPS is the classic breakaway and D-limonene-soluble support for the ABS family; it is documented for base ABS and only inferred for this filled grade (unverified). PLA and PETG pair badly in either direction, as for base ABS: a 100 °C bed and 260 °C nozzle deform them and the chemistries do not fuse. Not listed as a support for other materials — it welds to its own family rather than releasing from it.

plate_recommendations.notes: Upgraded from base ABS's 'usable' to 'recommended' because the fiber cuts the corner-lift that makes unfilled ABS marginal on textured PEI — but still use an adhesion aid. Bambu's 80-100 °C bed guidance explicitly assumes glue, and vendor listings in this category commonly specify glue-assisted adhesion at the 80-110 °C bed range. Brims help on large footprints.

emissions.notes: Inherits base ABS's emission profile unchanged — styrene plus very high ultrafine-particle rates, the worst class in this cluster alongside asa-cf and far above the PET/PETG-family entries. Print in a vented enclosure or filter through HEPA plus activated carbon, and never in an occupied unventilated room. Siraya claims 'minimized odour' for its Fibreheart grade specifically; that is a brand claim, not an independently verified or general glass-fiber effect, and should not change how the material is ventilated. Glass fiber dust from sanding or drilling is a separate skin and respiratory irritant.

safety_notes: Styrene is a respiratory irritant and a suspected carcinogen with chronic exposure — ventilation is not optional. Abrasive: hardened steel nozzle mandatory. Glass fiber fines from sanding, drilling or cutting irritate skin, eyes and airways; wear a mask and gloves and capture dust. Not food-contact suitable.
additional_notes: Choose between the two filled styrenics on UV exposure alone: abs-gf and asa-cf print almost identically and cost very differently, but ABS's polybutadiene rubber yellows and embrittles in sunlight while ASA's acrylate rubber does not. Indoors, abs-gf gives most of asa-cf's dimensional benefit at roughly a third of the price; outdoors it is the wrong material at any price. Glass-fiber percentage is inconsistently labelled across brands — a product named 'ABS-GF25' may or may not carry 25 % fiber — so verify loading per product before relying on a mechanical number.

provenance.conflicts: Tensile strength disagrees between the two primary vendors — Bambu 36±3 MPa, Siraya Fibreheart 44±3 MPa — a spread wide enough that it most likely reflects different glass loadings or test methods rather than noise; the recorded 33-47 MPa band spans both. Bed temperature likewise splits (Bambu 80-100 °C with glue, Siraya 100-110 °C) and softening/HDT splits 99-103 °C (Bambu) against 106 °C (Siraya). Glass-fiber content is genuinely unclear across the category: ~10 % is documented for Fibreheart while 'ABS-GF25' branding implies 25 % without substantiation. Bambu's ABS-GF technical data sheet returned 402 on fetch, so its figures come from cached search results and the store page rather than the PDF itself. AMS status is unusual and brand-specific — Bambu allows its own grade on AMS and AMS lite while third-party fiber-filled filament is generally barred — recorded 'conditional'. HIPS as a support is documented for base ABS and inferred here. Shrinkage is reasoned from the 'minimal warping' marketing claim, not measured.
